title: Rebekah at the well (Genesis 24)
hookLine: a servant prays for a sign, and a young woman waters ten camels

lines: A ROAD TRIP FOR A WIFE.
HE STOPS AT THE WELL AND PRAYS.
cards: Genesis twenty-four is a road trip. Abraham is old, Sarah is buried, and Isaac is grown, and alone.

So Abraham sends his oldest servant, the one who runs everything, back to the old country to find Isaac a wife among his own family. The servant loads ten camels with gifts and sets out for Mesopotamia.
At evening he reaches a well outside the city of Nahor, when the women come out to draw water. And before he does anything else, he stops and prays. Not for a beautiful bride.

teach.b: Here's the sign he asks for, in the King James Bible: let the young woman I ask for a drink say, "Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also." Anyone might give a stranger a sip of water.
But a thirsty camel drinks a great deal, and he has ten. Watering them all means trip after trip to the spring with a heavy jar, for a man she's never met. He isn't asking for luck.
He's asking for character: generosity beyond what's asked. Before he has done speaking, the text says, Rebekah comes out with her jar on her shoulder. He asks for a little water.
She says, drink, my lord, and lowers her jar. Then, unprompted: "I will draw water for thy camels also, until they have done drinking."
She runs, again and again, until ten camels are done, while the servant watches, silent, amazed. In his prayer he asked God to show kindness to his master.
The Hebrew word is chesed, loyal, generous love that goes beyond duty, and it runs all through this chapter. One more thing.

teach.h: WILT THOU GO? I WILL GO.
teach.b: When her family asks, "Wilt thou go with this man?", she answers, "I will go." In Hebrew that's a single word, elekh, from the same verb God used when he told Abraham to go.
The chapter ends at evening, far south, where Isaac has gone out into a field.

teach.h: I WILL DRAW WATER FOR THY CAMELS ALSO.
teach.b: He sees camels coming. He marries Rebekah, he loves her, and he is comforted after his mother's death.

how: Many Christians pray for guidance before big decisions, as Abraham's servant did, and the story of Rebekah is sometimes read at weddings and in teaching on generosity and hospitality.

games.q: you're at the well with your jar. a tired stranger with ten camels asks you for a little water. what do you do?
o: give him a sip and go home.
give him a drink, then water all ten camels until they're done.
point him to the next well.
games.why: "I will draw water for thy camels also, until they have done drinking." trip after trip, for a man she's never met.

practice: Small requests are coming your way: can you grab me a glass of water, can you send that file?
Pick one and imagine Rebekah's answer, yes, and also: fill the glass and refill the pitcher, send the file and a note that saves them time. If you pray, you can ask for a generous heart.

wordCard.voice: Chesed. Hebrew for loyal, generous love that goes beyond duty: what the servant saw when Rebekah offered to water ten camels.

orig.note: Hebrew: loyal, generous love, kindness that goes beyond duty. It runs through Genesis 24.

carryVoice: Your line: kindness to camels. One more trip to the well than anyone asked for. See you tomorrow.
